US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.
The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, would "support America's booming super intelligence economy".
There is increasing opposition to data centres on earth, including in the US where experts say they were a factor in the Republicans big losses in the midterm elections.
SpaceX believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".

article.title: Pollution Driven by U.S. Data Centers Causing Hundreds of Early Deaths
article.summary:
U.S. data centers are driving greater power demand, and with it, more pollution from coal and gas power plants.
The new modeling study finds that, in 2023, the added power demand from data centers led to an estimated 650 early deaths across the U.S.
Given the rapid buildout of data centers, their impact would likely be even greater today, authors say.
The study further suggests that pollution is often intensifying far from where data centers are located.
In Oregon and Virginia, two data center hotspots, they are consuming more than 15 percent of the electricity sold in each state.

article.title: Russia's own figures show it has lost nearly 500,000 people in Ukraine war
article.summary:
At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.
The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.
Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday that only Russia's defence ministry could officially report data on losses: "I suggest no other data be taken into account."
The defence ministry has not released any official casualty figures for several years.

article.summary:

"What good has President [Donald] Trump done the United States and, by extension, the world - was he a change or a step backwards?"
he asked supporters, before invoking the administrations of Brazil's former leader, Jair Bolsonaro, and Argentinian President Javier Milei.
The election comes amid a deeply polarised political atmosphere in which both left and right have warned about their opponents' ability to undermine democracy.
In a Europe dominated by right-leaning governments, Sánchez has gained a reputation as the continent's most outspoken and uncompromising left-wing prime minister.

article.summary:

Malaysia will send more than 6,500 Rohingya refugees back to Myanmar in a new round of repatriations, said Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.

article.title: What Australia’s ‘Digital Duty of Care’ Law Means for Big Tech
article.summary:
Under the Digital Duty of Care law, platforms must provide risk assessments to regulators at least once a year, and they must notify regulators before they introduce significant changes to their platforms that could allow for new risks of harm, such as “addictive” design features.
The amendments also make it easier for Australian citizens to hold tech companies to account.
Previously, one needed to rely on complex legal avenues concerning company negligence and consumer protection.
The new law grants Australians the “private right of action,” which means they can directly sue digital platforms for breaching their duty of care.

article.title: North Korea expels Swiss diplomat in sanctions row
article.summary:
North Korea has ordered Switzerland's diplomatic representative to leave the country within 48 hours and called for the office to close, in a row over sanctions.
Confirming the expulsion, KCNA said: "The Foreign Ministry of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) declared the head of the Swiss Diplomatic Office in the DPRK persona non grata and urged him to leave the country within 48 hours."
The diplomatic rebuke comes weeks after Swiss foreign minister Ignazio Cassis made a rare visit to North Korea, where he officially reopened the office and discussed normalising relations.
Swiss authorities said relations between the two countries would be maintained through the North Korean embassy in Bern, and the Swiss embassy in Beijing.
Diplomatic links with North Korea were first established in 1974 and Switzerland opened a co-operation office in Pyongyang in 1997.
